description:
Hi! We're a team of two siblings from Instituto Salesiano San Miguel, in Honduras, and we love space! We're Edgar (11), and Isabella (9). We really like studying, especially math, and everything about the universe — planets, rockets, astronauts, and how everything works up there. We love asking questions, solving challenges, and discovering new things together.

Why join our team? We're responsible, we work well as a team, and we always help each other out. We like thinking with numbers, but we also love inventing and creating new ideas. We want to make an awesome project and have lots of fun learning along the way!

What are we looking for in a teammate? We'd love someone who knows how to code, someone creative who can help with drawings or the presentation, and someone who loves researching space stuff.
summary: Rover’s Talent Show is an interactive storybook, written and drawn by two kids, Edgar and Isabella, that introduces children to the robots NASA left on Mars. Narizón, a giant Deep Space Network antenna with a long, pointy nose, picks up a signal from Curiosity, who is hosting a talent show for the robots that no longer move: Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity and InSight, plus Kepler as a special guest from deep space. Each robot tells its own story and shows off the science it made possible. Every number in the book comes from NASA, every scene links to the real data, and readers can spin NASA’s official 3D models of the robots. The story ends with all of them saying together: “We are abandoned, but not forgotten!” After the last page, readers can play the Mars Rovers Game, created by Edgar.
details:
What it does. Our project is a storybook that you read in the browser, and its pages turn like a real book. Each page pair has our original drawing with comic speech bubbles on the left, and the story, the mission facts and a hands-on activity on the right. Readers meet one robot per scene, learn when it landed, how long NASA planned for it to work and how long it really lasted. Then they press a button to see its “talent”:

•  Sojourner races across a classroom at 1 centimeter per second.

•  Spirit drags its broken wheel and uncovers silica, a clue that Mars once had hot water.

• Oppy runs a 42.195-kilometer marathon that took 11 years and 2 months.

• Ingenuity counts up to its 72 flights, when it was only asked for 5.

• InSight feels a marsquake.

•  Kepler shows how a planet passing in front of its star makes the light dim.

A “See me in 3D!” button opens NASA’s official 3D model of each robot. Readers can rotate and zoom it, and for Spirit and Opportunity they can also see real photos taken from orbit by the HiRISE camera. The book ends with a scoreboard, a quiz and a page about our team.

Why it matters. When a mission ends, the rover stays on Mars, and most kids never hear about it again. We wanted to show that these robots are not junk: each one gave scientists something important. A talent show is a format kids already understand, and the characters are drawn by kids, so other kids can see themselves in the story. The scoreboard makes a big idea easy to see: every robot worked much longer than NASA planned. Opportunity lasted about 57 times longer than its 90-sol mission.

Who it is for. Children from about 7 to 12 years old, their teachers and their families. The book works on a computer or a tablet, does not need an account, and the activities can be used in a classroom.

How we built it. First we chose the challenge and invented the characters, and then we drew every scene by hand. We wrote the dialogues in our own words. We checked every fact against NASA mission pages and reports. The book is a single web page built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The 3D models are NASA’s GLB files, shown with the three.js library.

Tools and technologies. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, three.js, NASA 3D Resources (GLB models), Google Fonts, paper, pencils and markers.
